children.text: The historical ATLAS model uses a uniform B=2.00 T solenoidal field in a cylinder of radius R=1.10 m. Electrons start at its centre. Use m=9.11×10^−31 kg, e=1.60×10^−19 C, c=3.00×10^8 m/s and ε0=8.85×10^−12 F/m. For perpendicular acceleration the radiated power is \(P=e^2a^2\gamma^4/(6\pi\epsilon_0c^3)\). Part B reconstructs a neutrino from \(t\to bW^+\to b\mu^+\nu\). Treat all final particles and jets as massless. Their measured momenta (px,py,pz), in GeV/c, are: anti-muon (−24.7,−24.9,−12.4), jet 1 (−14.2,50.1,94.1), neutrino (−104.1,5.3,unknown). The neutrino transverse components come from missing transverse momentum. Do not assume zero total longitudinal momentum. Use mW=80.4 GeV/c² and rest-frame top lifetime 5×10^−25 s.
For a nonrelativistic electron with kinetic energy K, derive its radius r.
What minimum momentum lets an electron produced at the centre reach the cylindrical boundary? Give MeV/c.
An electron starts radially with 100 GeV energy. Estimate the positive energy lost before escape, in MeV.
Find the ultrarelativistic cyclotron angular frequency ω(t), using α from A4.

statement.text:
Where is the neutrino?
The historical ATLAS model uses a uniform B=2.00 T solenoidal field in a cylinder of radius R=1.10 m. Electrons start at its centre. Use m=9.11×10^−31 kg, e=1.60×10^−19 C, c=3.00×10^8 m/s and ε0=8.85×10^−12 F/m. For perpendicular acceleration the radiated power is \(P=e^2a^2\gamma^4/(6\pi\epsilon_0c^3)\). Part B reconstructs a neutrino from \(t\to bW^+\to b\mu^+\nu\). Treat all final particles and jets as massless. Their measured momenta (px,py,pz), in GeV/c, are: anti-muon (−24.7,−24.9,−12.4), jet 1 (−14.2,50.1,94.1), neutrino (−104.1,5.3,unknown). The neutrino transverse components come from missing transverse momentum. Do not assume zero total longitudinal momentum. Use mW=80.4 GeV/c² and rest-frame top lifetime 5×10^−25 s.
a.1. Classical cyclotron radius
For a nonrelativistic electron with kinetic energy K, derive its radius r.
a.2. Escape momentum
What minimum momentum lets an electron produced at the centre reach the cylindrical boundary? Give MeV/c.
a.3. Ultrarelativistic radiation
Write \(P=\xi e^4E^2B^2/(\epsilon_0m^kc^n)\). Find ξ,k,n.
a.4. Energy loss coefficient
In \(E(t)=E_0/(1+\alpha E_0t)\), find α.
a.5. Radiated energy on escape
An electron starts radially with 100 GeV energy. Estimate the positive energy lost before escape, in MeV.
a.6. Time-dependent angular frequency
Find the ultrarelativistic cyclotron angular frequency ω(t), using α from A4.
b.1. W mass constraint

Derive the equation for mW² in terms of the anti-muon and neutrino transverse vectors and their longitudinal components.
b.2. Two neutrino solutions
Solve the W mass constraint for both possible neutrino pz values.
b.3. Reconstructed top masses
Calculate the top mass for each neutrino solution. If necessary use approximate fallback pz=70 and −180 GeV/c and state that choice.
b.4. Select the likely candidate

Use the supplied top-mass distribution to choose a candidate and estimate its normalized signal weight, called probability in the source.
b.5. Distance before decay
For the likely candidate, calculate the mean laboratory distance travelled before decay.

children.text: The track's largest radial distance is twice its curvature radius, so r=R/2=0.55 m. The relativistic relation p=eBr gives p≈330 MeV/c.
For v≈c, \(a=ecB/(\gamma m)\) and E=γmc². Substitution yields \(P=e^4E^2B^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5)\). Thus ξ=1/(6π), k=4, n=5.
Integrating \(\dot E=-\alpha E^2\) gives the stated law with \(\alpha=e^4B^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5)\).

Its curvature radius is about 167 m, so flight time is R/c. Loss \(E_0-E(R/c)\simeq\alpha E_0^2R/c\simeq56\,\mathrm{MeV}\). The signed energy change is −56 MeV, while the requested lost energy is positive.

For each root add the three final energies \(E_t=c(p_\mu+p_\nu+p_j)\) and vectors \(\mathbf p_t=\mathbf p_\mu+\mathbf p_\nu+\mathbf p_j\). Then \(m_t=c^{-2}\sqrt{E_t^2-c^2p_t^2}\). The exact-root candidates are about 169.3 and 311.2 GeV/c² respectively. Rounded fallback roots give nearby but different values.

The dashed signal curve is about 0.1 near 169.3 GeV/c² and below 0.01 near 311.2 GeV/c², favouring the positive-pz candidate. The plotted normalized bin weight is roughly 0.1. It is not a posterior probability between the two candidates without an additional likelihood model.
Its energy is about 272.6 GeV. Time dilation gives \(d=v\gamma\tau_0=(p_t/m_t)\tau_0=c\tau_0\sqrt{[E_t/(m_tc^2)]^2-1}\simeq2\times10^{-16}\,\mathrm m\).

solution.text:
Where is the neutrino?
a.1. Classical cyclotron radius
From \(evB=mv^2/r\) and \(K=mv^2/2\), \(r=\sqrt{2mK}/(eB)\).
a.2. Escape momentum
The track's largest radial distance is twice its curvature radius, so r=R/2=0.55 m. The relativistic relation p=eBr gives p≈330 MeV/c.
a.3. Ultrarelativistic radiation
For v≈c, \(a=ecB/(\gamma m)\) and E=γmc². Substitution yields \(P=e^4E^2B^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5)\). Thus ξ=1/(6π), k=4, n=5.
a.4. Energy loss coefficient
Integrating \(\dot E=-\alpha E^2\) gives the stated law with \(\alpha=e^4B^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5)\).
a.5. Radiated energy on escape
Its curvature radius is about 167 m, so flight time is R/c. Loss \(E_0-E(R/c)\simeq\alpha E_0^2R/c\simeq56\,\mathrm{MeV}\). The signed energy change is −56 MeV, while the requested lost energy is positive.
a.6. Time-dependent angular frequency
\(r=p/(eB)\), p≈E/c, hence \(\omega=c/r=ec^2B/E(t)=ec^2B(1+\alpha E_0t)/E_0\).
b.1. W mass constraint
Add their four-momenta and use zero individual masses: \[m_W^2c^2=2\left[p_\mu\sqrt{p_{\nu T}^2+p_{\nu z}^2}-\mathbf p_{\mu T}\cdot\mathbf p_{\nu T}-p_{\mu z}p_{\nu z}\right],\quad p_\mu=\sqrt{p_{\mu T}^2+p_{\mu z}^2}.\]
b.2. Two neutrino solutions
Let \(A=m_W^2c^2/2+\mathbf p_{\mu T}\cdot\mathbf p_{\nu T}\). Squaring \(p_\mu\sqrt{p_{\nu T}^2+z^2}=A+p_{\mu z}z\) gives \[p_{\mu T}^2z^2-2Ap_{\mu z}z+p_\mu^2p_{\nu T}^2-A^2=0.\] Check both roots in the unsquared equation. They are approximately +74.0 and −188.3 GeV/c.
b.3. Reconstructed top masses
For each root add the three final energies \(E_t=c(p_\mu+p_\nu+p_j)\) and vectors \(\mathbf p_t=\mathbf p_\mu+\mathbf p_\nu+\mathbf p_j\). Then \(m_t=c^{-2}\sqrt{E_t^2-c^2p_t^2}\). The exact-root candidates are about 169.3 and 311.2 GeV/c² respectively. Rounded fallback roots give nearby but different values.
b.4. Select the likely candidate
The dashed signal curve is about 0.1 near 169.3 GeV/c² and below 0.01 near 311.2 GeV/c², favouring the positive-pz candidate. The plotted normalized bin weight is roughly 0.1. It is not a posterior probability between the two candidates without an additional likelihood model.
b.5. Distance before decay
Its energy is about 272.6 GeV. Time dilation gives \(d=v\gamma\tau_0=(p_t/m_t)\tau_0=c\tau_0\sqrt{[E_t/(m_tc^2)]^2-1}\simeq2\times10^{-16}\,\mathrm m\).
